2026-11-08.title: Thirty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: Wisdom is found by those who seek her
My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God
God will bring with him those who have died
2026-11-08.alt: Year A, the last Sundays of the liturgical year. Shorter form of the Second Reading: 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14.
2026-11-08.verse: Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
theo: As the liturgical year draws to its close, the readings turn our eyes to the end: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and our readiness. The tone is not fear but longing. The psalm sets it: “O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you.” Wisdom, says the first reading, is not hard to find for those who love her: “she will be found sitting at the gate”.

The parable of the ten bridesmaids is about a wedding, the great biblical image of God's covenant love. All ten are invited; all ten have lamps; all ten fall asleep. The difference is the oil. The wise brought flasks with their lamps; the foolish did not. When the cry comes at midnight, “Look! Here is the bridegroom!”, the oil cannot be borrowed. Some things no one can do for us: our own faith, our own prayer, our own charity.

The Fathers asked what the oil means. St Augustine saw it as charity; others saw good works, or the grace of the Holy Spirit kept alive by prayer. All agree that it is something gathered slowly, day by day, not bought in a hurry at the last moment. The Catechism reminds us that each person receives his eternal retribution at death, in a particular judgement (CCC 1022). Readiness is not a single act but a habit.

Paul gives the hope behind the vigilance. The Thessalonians grieved for members who had died before Christ's return. Paul says: do not grieve “as others do who have no hope”. Since Jesus died and rose, God will bring with him those who have died, “and so we will be with the Lord forever”. The bridegroom is coming not to catch us out but to take us in.
conn: In Jesus' time the bridegroom went to fetch his bride from her father's house, and the procession to his home often happened at night by torchlight. Delays were common while the families settled the details. Bridesmaids waited to escort him with lamps.
The Greek lampades probably means torches: sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags, which burned out in about fifteen minutes. Without a supply of oil they were useless.
The same words appear in Matthew 7:23 for those who said “Lord, Lord” without doing the Father's will. Being near Jesus is not the same as knowing him.
In Wisdom 6 and Proverbs 8 Wisdom is a woman who seeks people out. The Fathers saw in her a figure of Christ, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).
1 Thessalonians (c. AD 50) contains the earliest written Christian teaching on the resurrection of the dead and the coming of the Lord.

The early Church prayed in Aramaic, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20). Every Mass keeps the prayer: “as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ.”
altar: At every Mass, after the Our Father, the priest prays that we may be kept safe “as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ”. The Eucharist is the wedding banquet tasted in advance.
The sanctuary lamp burning beside the tabernacle is a silent bridesmaid: it keeps watch day and night before the Lord. Let our hearts be like it.
outline: Ask: if Christ came tonight at midnight, would your lamp be burning?
Point 1 · Wisdom waits at the gate
God is not hard to find for those who seek him.
Faith, prayer and charity are gathered day by day; no one can give us theirs.
We wait not in fear but in hope; the dead in Christ will rise.
The sanctuary lamp that never goes out.
“Keep awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
live: Add one small daily habit of prayer this week and keep it.
Give God the first five minutes of your morning.
Visit or call a family that lost someone this year.
Make Sunday Mass the fixed centre of your week.
fathers: In a sermon on this parable he says the oil is charity: the lamps of good works must burn with love, not for human praise.
He notes that the foolish virgins had kept virginity, a great thing, yet lacked mercy toward the poor; without charity even great virtues fail.
He teaches that the oil of the wise is the inner glory of conscience, which no one else can lend.
magis: The Last Judgement and the return of Christ.
saints: 9 Nov: Dedication of the Lateran Basilica. 10 Nov: St Leo the Great. 11 Nov: St Martin of Tours. 12 Nov: St Josaphat.
2026-11-08.prayer: Almighty and merciful God, graciously keep from us all adversity, so that, unhindered in mind and body alike, we may pursue in freedom of heart the things that are yours. Keep our lamps burning until the Bridegroom comes. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: God is easily found by those who seek him.
Oil cannot be borrowed: no one can pray or love for us.
The Bridegroom comes to take us in, not to catch us out.

2026-11-08.question: Is my lamp burning, or only lit for show?
2026-11-08.special: Thirty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year A. The last Sundays of the year turn our attention to the end of time and the coming of Christ.
illus: In many Kerala homes the evening lamp (nilavilakku) is lit at dusk and the family gathers to pray. Someone must remember to buy oil and trim the wick every day. A lamp left empty one evening does not light just because the family is in a hurry.

family.explain: Ten girls waited for a wedding. Five had extra oil for their lamps and five did not. When the bridegroom came, only the ready ones went in. Jesus wants us to be ready by loving him every day.
family.intention: We pray to be always ready to meet Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the ‘oil’ in our family's lamp?”

kidsaint: A Roman soldier who cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar. That night he dreamed of Jesus wearing the half-cloak. Lesson: what we do for the poor, we do for Jesus.
term: Greek for “presence” or “arrival”, used of the glorious return of Christ at the end of time (CCC 1001; 1040).

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, every Malayali knows what it is to wait for a wedding procession. Today Jesus tells a story about ten young women waiting for the bridegroom.

All ten were invited. All ten had lamps. And all ten fell asleep, because the bridegroom was late. Jesus does not blame them for sleeping. The difference was simple: five had brought extra oil, and five had not.

At midnight the cry went up: “Look! Here is the bridegroom!” The foolish ones said, “Give us some of your oil.” But the wise could not. Why? Because some things cannot be shared at the last moment. My faith cannot replace yours. My prayer cannot be your prayer. The Fathers said the oil is charity, good works, the life of grace. These are gathered slowly, drop by drop, day by day.

The first reading says Wisdom is easy to find: “she will be found sitting at the gate.” God is not hiding. He is waiting at the door of our day. Those who rise early to seek him find him. So the question is not whether God is available, but whether we go to him.

And St Paul reminds us why we wait with hope and not fear. Some in Thessalonica had lost loved ones. Paul says: do not grieve as those who have no hope. Jesus died and rose, and those who died in him will rise with him, “and so we will be with the Lord forever.” This November, as we pray for our dead, these words are our comfort.

So let us fill our flasks this week. A few minutes of prayer each morning. A Sunday Mass that is never missed. A kindness to someone in need. Drop by drop, the lamp is filled. And when the Bridegroom comes, may he find our lamps burning.
kids: Children, have you ever waited for a guest who was late?
Jesus told a story about ten girls waiting for a bridegroom with lamps. Five brought extra oil, and five forgot.
The oil is like our love for Jesus: we fill it up a little every day when we pray and are kind.
Tonight, before sleeping, say: “Jesus, I love you. Keep my lamp burning!”

intro: Wisdom waits at the gate; the oil of faith and love is gathered daily; the Bridegroom comes in hope.

q: Wisdom is radiant and unfading, and she is easily discerned by those who love her, and is found by those who seek her. She hastens to make herself known to those who desire her. One who rises early to seek her will have no difficulty, for she will be found sitting at the gate.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
points.apply: Give God the first five minutes of each morning.

sub: All ten slept; five had oil.
Faith, prayer and charity are personal.
They are gathered drop by drop.
q: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
But the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.
points.apply: Add one daily habit of prayer and keep it.

sub: He comes to take us in.
The dead in Christ will rise.
q: For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your builder marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.
And while they went to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut.
points.apply: Pray “Come, Lord Jesus” each night this week.

concl: Readiness is a habit, not a last-minute act.
Let us fill our flasks today.
2026-11-08.resolve: Never miss Sunday Mass this month.
